entry.title: FastAPI Source Tour: How Requests, Dependencies and OpenAPI Are Wired Together

link.title: FastAPI Source Tour: How Requests, Dependencies and OpenAPI Are Wired Together

entry.content:
FastAPI has quietly become the default answer to “how do I expose this Python function over HTTP?” — for data science teams shipping models, for backend teams building microservices, and increasingly for LLM tooling that needs a clean JSON surface. The project sits at version 0.162.0 as of this writing, and unlike many popular frameworks, its source tree is small enough to read in an afternoon. That is exactly what this post does: we clone the repository, open the handful of files that carry the whole framework, and trace one HTTP request from the ASGI entry point down to the serialized JSON response.

What makes FastAPI worth reading at the source level is that it is deliberately a thin, opinionated layer over two other projects. Starlette provides the ASGI application, routing primitives, middleware and response objects. Pydantic — which we covered separately in our Pydantic tour — provides data models, validation and serialization. FastAPI’s own code is mostly about the glue: declaring parameters declaratively, resolving dependencies per request, and generating a machine-readable OpenAPI schema from everything it learns about your functions. Because the layer is thin, every surprising behavior you meet in day-to-day coding has a short, findable explanation in the source.

The two diagrams below were generated from the actual repository at commit time. The first gives the five-region overview; the second drills into thirty-four symbols across seven regions, distinguishing what happens once at registration time from what happens on every request. Every node in the SVGs links into the real source on GitHub, at the line numbers verified with grep while writing this post.

Figure 1 — FastAPI overview: the application object, the routing layer, the dependency-injection engine, the OpenAPI/Docs region, and the response-encoding region. Click any node to open the exact source file on GitHub.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • class FastAPI, L52 — the application you instantiate; a Starlette subclass that adds parameter validation, dependency injection and OpenAPI generation on top of the parent’s ASGI machinery.
  • APIRouter, L2327 — the registry behind every @app.get(...) and @router.post(...) decorator; it owns the list of routes and the logic for merging routers together.
  • APIRoute, L1179 — one path operation. It computes the dependency tree for its endpoint exactly once, at registration time, then reuses that tree for every request.
  • get_request_handler, L397 — the factory that returns the per-request closure: solve dependencies, await your endpoint, serialize the result.
  • solve_dependencies, L643 — the runtime heart of the DI engine, resolving your declared dependencies (and their sub-dependencies) with caching.
  • get_openapi, L577 — introspects the same routes you registered and emits the OpenAPI 3.1 document served at /openapi.json.
  • get_swagger_ui_html, L40 — renders the interactive /docs page that consumes that schema, so documentation is a byproduct of routing, not a separate artifact.

Starlette Below, FastAPI Above

The first thing the source confirms is that FastAPI does not reimplement an HTTP framework. class FastAPI(Starlette) inherits the ASGI callable protocol, the middleware stack and the router plumbing. What the subclass adds is visible in four methods. The constructor at applications.py, L68 accepts the metadata you know from every tutorial — title, version, openapi_url, dependencies, lifespan — and then calls setup() at L1120, which registers the /openapi.json, /docs and /redoc routes on the internal router. build_middleware_stack() at L1032 assembles ServerErrorMiddleware, your user middleware, ExceptionMiddleware and finally the router, in that order. And __call__ at L1175 is the ASGI entry point any server (Uvicorn, Hypercorn, or the fastapi CLI) invokes per connection.

The decorators are pure sugar. @app.get("/") resolves to the method at L1688, which forwards to add_api_route at L1207, which delegates to the same-named method on APIRouter. include_router at L1483 is the same delegation pattern for whole routers, which is why prefixes, tags and router-level dependencies compose the way the tutorials promise. There is no hidden second registration path — everything funnels through one method on one router.

How a Request Actually Travels

With the route registered, a request enters through request_response at routing.py, L129, which adapts the handler — sync or async — into a Starlette-compatible ASGI callable. The real work happens in the closure returned by get_request_handler: it calls solve_dependencies to produce the keyword arguments your function declared, awaits the endpoint, then hands the return value to serialize_response at L320. If you declared a response_model, that function validates the raw result against it and filters out any extra fields — the validation here is the same Pydantic machinery used on input, just in the outbound direction. The validated object goes through jsonable_encoder, L129, which recursively converts Pydantic models, dataclasses, enums and datetimes into JSON-safe structures.

Failure paths are equally explicit. HTTPException at exceptions.py, L17 and RequestValidationError at L212 are converted to JSON by the handlers in exception_handlers.py, and both are installed by the middleware stack built at startup. Side effects that must not delay the response — sending an email, writing a log line — are attached to a BackgroundTasks object (class at background.py, L12), which the DI engine will happily inject as a parameter; the tasks run after the response has been sent. There is even an SSE-shaped escape hatch: EventSourceResponse at sse.py, L20 is a StreamingResponse subclass that formats server-sent events for you.

The Dependency Injection Engine

The dependency system is the part most worth reading because it is the least documented by intuition. At registration time, get_dependant at dependencies/utils.py, L300 walks the endpoint’s signature using get_typed_signature at L242 and produces a Dependant — a dataclass at dependencies/models.py, L32 that holds the callable, its sub-dependencies, and every parameter classified by kind. The classifier is analyze_param at L409: a parameter is a path segment, a query string, a header, a cookie, a request-body field, or itself a dependency, decided by what you wrapped it in.

Those wrappers live in params.py: Depends at line 791, Body at 498, Query at 232, Path at 142, Header at 320, with Form and File deriving from Body, and Security deriving from Depends to carry scope requirements. The friendlier function API you actually type — Depends(...), Query(...), Body(...) — lives in param_functions.py and simply constructs those classes. At request time, solve_dependencies walks the tree recursively, caches results per request (so an expensive dependency used in three places runs once), and collects validation errors from all branches before failing, which is why error responses list every bad field at once rather than just the first.

This design has a pleasant consequence: the same engine serves the docs. get_openapi_path at openapi/utils.py, L303 reads the very same Dependant objects to emit parameter and request-body schemas, so what /docs shows is guaranteed to match what your endpoint accepts. If you have used model servers that expose LLM endpoints over HTTP — say behind LiteLLM gateways or inside Open WebUI — you have consumed APIs whose documentation quality depends on exactly this kind of schema-from-code generation.

From Install to Your First Model

Everything above is easier to internalize once you have the minimal app running. The steps below follow the repository’s own README exactly.

First, install the standard distribution into a virtual environment: pip install "fastapi[standard]". The [standard] extra pulls in uvicorn[standard] for the ASGI server plus the CLI tooling, so you get the batteries-included experience the docs assume.

Second, create a file main.py with the README’s example — this is the whole thing:

from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/")
def read_root():
    return {"Hello": "World"}


@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
def read_item(item_id: int, q: str | None = None):
    return {"item_id": item_id, "q": q}

Third, run it with fastapi dev (or uv run fastapi dev if you use uv). The CLI reads main.py automatically, detects the app, starts Uvicorn on http://127.0.0.1:8000 with auto-reload in development mode, and prints the /docs URL alongside it. The README notes that for production you switch to fastapi run. Open /items/5?q=somequery and you will see the JSON response; open /docs and you will see Swagger UI rendering the schema that get_openapi generated from those two decorators — the source tour and the tutorial are the same story told at two altitudes.

The Detail Diagram: Registration Time vs Request Time

The single most useful mental model the source gives you is the split between what happens once, when the route is registered, and what happens per request. The detail diagram below makes that split explicit: the upper region (application and routing) mostly runs at import time, the middle regions (dependency resolution and parameter classification) have a registration phase and a request phase, and the OpenAPI region reads only registration-time facts.

Figure 2 — FastAPI in detail: 34 symbols across 7 regions, from FastAPI.__init__ and build_middleware_stack down to analyze_param, jsonable_encoder and the exception handlers. Node links go to the exact lines on GitHub.

Two details reward attention here. First, APIRoute exposes get_route_handler at routing.py, L1278 as an official override point — subclass APIRoute, return a wrapped handler, and you can intercept every request to that route without touching middleware. Second, APIWebSocketRoute at L854 routes WebSocket connections through the same solve_dependencies engine, which is why WebSocket endpoints can declare Depends(...) parameters and get session-scoped caching for free.

Honest Limits

  • The speed claim is the README’s, not mine. The repository’s headline advertises high performance, and the framework does lean on Uvicorn, Pydantic and orjson/ujson response classes (ORJSONResponse, L78), but the source contains no benchmarks. If throughput matters to you, measure your own workload; the framework will not do it for you.
  • It is an API framework first. Server-rendered HTML is possible via Starlette’s templating integration, but the core — validation, DI, OpenAPI — is built around JSON request/response cycles. If you want a content site, this is the wrong tool; if you want an API consumed by tools like txt.ai’s semantic search or an MCP server built with the MCP Python SDK, it is the right one.
  • The magic is signature-based. DI works by inspecting type hints at import time, so refactorings that rename parameters or change types silently change runtime behavior. Static analyzers see less than the runtime does, and circular dependencies between modules surface as confusing signature errors rather than clean import loops.
  • No user management, no ORM, no cache. The fastapi.security package provides credential extractors (HTTP Basic, OAuth2 bearer flows, API keys), not an auth system. You bring your own database layer, session store and permission model.
  • Line numbers drift. Every link in this post was verified against master at the version above; a few minor releases from now, functions will have moved. The diagrams were generated from the same commit, so clicking through the SVGs will always re-anchor you.

Where to Go Next

If this tour changed how you read framework code, the natural next steps are: read Pydantic’s own source tour to understand the validation layer FastAPI leans on; look at how LiteLLM standardizes provider APIs behind one OpenAI-shaped surface you could serve with FastAPI; or study Open WebUI for a full product built on top of this stack. For semantic search backends, txt.ai pairs naturally with a FastAPI front door, and the MCP Python SDK shows the same declarative-function-over-protocol pattern applied to tool servers.
entry.summary: A line-by-line tour of the FastAPI source tree on GitHub: the Starlette core, the APIRouter machinery, the dependency injection engine, OpenAPI generation and response encoding, with interactive architecture diagrams.

entry.title: huggingface_hub: A Source Tour of the Python Client Behind the Hugging Face Hub

link.title: huggingface_hub: A Source Tour of the Python Client Behind the Hugging Face Hub

entry.content:
Every time you call from_pretrained in [transformers](/transformers/) — well, not quite. What actually fetches the weights is a smaller, quieter package underneath: huggingface_hub. It is the client library that speaks to the Hub's REST API, moves terabytes of model weights onto your disk, keeps a content-addressed cache consistent, and hands you typed metadata objects when you go looking for models. Transformers, [datasets](/datasets/), diffusers, and a large part of the modern open-source ML ecosystem all sit on top of it.

In this post we read the huggingface_hub source the way a maintainer would: top-down, starting from the public surface, then descending into the download path, the upload path, and the plumbing that ties them together. Every symbol mentioned below is linked to the exact line in the repository at main as of October 2026, so you can click through and see the same code we describe. Two diagrams anchor the tour — a compact overview and a denser detail map — both generated from the real file tree, with clickable nodes.

The first thing that stands out in the source tree is how flat it is. There is no deep hierarchy of frameworks; src/huggingface_hub/ holds a handful of purposeful modules: hf_api.py for REST verbs, file_download.py for the download path, _commit_api.py for uploads, hf_file_system.py for the fsspec bridge, plus a utils/ package for HTTP, auth, and cache helpers. One __init__.py re-exports the stable surface so that from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download is all you ever need to type.

Overview of huggingface_hub at main: the hf CLI and the Python API share one implementation core; downloads flow through hf_hub_download, uploads through commit operations, and everything rides on the shared HTTP, auth, and constants layer. Nodes are clickable and link into the repository.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The hf CLI, L54 is the terminal face of the library — its typer app drives the same Python API rather than duplicating it, which is why hf download and hf_hub_download always behave identically.
  • The init re-exports, L1050 define the stable import surface; the module list there is effectively the library’s public contract.
  • HfApi, L2127 is the REST client class — search, inspection, repo management — with methods like whoami, L2219 and list_models, L2311.
  • The download side is led by hf_hub_download, L857 for single files and snapshot_download, L123 for whole revisions.
  • The upload side is CommitOperationAdd, L141 and friends — uploads are modeled as commit operations, not ad-hoc HTTP calls.
  • HfFileSystem, L370 mounts Hub repositories as an fsspec filesystem, letting pandas-style random access work on remote repos.
  • All HTTP traffic funnels through http_backoff, L572, which adds retries and hands error mapping to hf_raise_for_status, L826.
  • Tokens are resolved by get_token, L60, and every default the library honors — ENDPOINT, L69, HF_HUB_CACHE, L177 — lives in constants.py.
  • Finally, InferenceClient, L124 covers the “run a model” story through Inference Providers.

The Detail View

Where the overview shows the shape of the library, the detail map below traces the actual call paths: how snapshot_download loops into hf_hub_download, how upload_file lowers into create_commit and commit operations, how the cache metadata is written, and where the Xet fast path hooks in.

The detail view: the download path (blue) resolves URLs and writes cache metadata; the upload path (green) serializes commit operations and picks LFS or Xet per file; the cache group (amber) shows the on-disk state; the infrastructure group carries auth, HTTP, and defaults.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps this part deliberately boring. Install the package (which also installs the hf CLI):

pip install huggingface_hub

Then pull a single file:

from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download

hf_hub_download(repo_id="zai-org/GLM-5.2", filename="config.json")

That one call does more than it looks. Internally, hf_hub_url, L211 builds the canonical resolve/<revision>/<filename> URL, an initial HEAD request reads the etag to learn whether the file changed, and only a cache miss triggers the actual download. The docstring of hf_hub_download, L857 spells out the cache layout it maintains: one folder per repo under the cache root, with blobs, refs, and snapshots subfolders, where snapshot filenames are relative links back into blobs. Pass local_dir=... instead and the repo’s file structure is replicated where you point it, with a .cache/huggingface/ metadata sidecar next to it instead of the central cache.

To grab an entire repository — weights, config, tokenizer, the lot — the README’s example is:

from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download

snapshot_download("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

snapshot_download, L123 lists the repo tree, applies any allow/deny patterns, then loops over the files with a thread pool, calling hf_hub_download for each. If you only want to know whether a file is already available offline, try_to_load_from_cache, L1523 answers that question without touching the network.

The same install also gives you the CLI, which the README demonstrates with a compact script: hf auth login to authenticate, hf models ls --warm to find models currently served by Inference Providers, hf download Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B to fetch weights, and hf upload username/my-cool-model ./model.safetensors to push one back. The CLI is built for humans and coding agents alike — the README even ships an hf skills add command that installs a command reference for AI agents.

Uploads Are Just Commit Operations

The download path is the one most people meet first, but the upload design is the more interesting half of the codebase. Creating a repo is a single call — create_repo, L4577 — and putting content into it works like this:

from huggingface_hub import upload_file

upload_file(
    path_or_fileobj="README.md",
    path_in_repo="README.md",
    repo_id="username/test-model",
)

Convenience functions like upload_file, L5604 and upload_folder, L5810 are thin wrappers: both lower into create_commit, L5018, passing a list of operations. An addition is described by CommitOperationAdd, L141, which computes a sha256 for the local file up front; deletions use CommitOperationDelete, L56; copies use CommitOperationCopy.

Before anything is sent, _fetch_upload_modes, L703 asks the Hub to classify each pending file: small files ride along inside the commit payload itself, while large ones are routed to either the classic LFS transfer (_upload_lfs_files, L465) or the newer Xet backend (_upload_xet_files, L552), which deduplicates content in chunks — the README credits Xet with making “file versioning, even for very large files” practical. Finally _prepare_commit_payload, L909 serializes everything and _send_commit, L1013 POSTs it. One atomic commit, identical semantics whether you uploaded one file or ten thousand.

Cache, Auth, and the Constants That Bind It Together

Three small modules do a disproportionate amount of work. First, constants.py: the Hub endpoint (ENDPOINT, L69, overridable via HF_ENDPOINT), the cache root (HF_HUB_CACHE, L177, overridable via HF_HUB_CACHE), and the various timeouts and limits every other module reads.

Second, the auth chain. login, L57 persists a user access token to a local token file; get_token, L60 then implements the resolution order — explicit argument, environment variable, stored token — so that a script written months ago keeps working after a re-login. Third, the disk-state helpers: files downloaded to a local_dir get their etag and commit hash recorded by write_download_metadata, L432, and the whole central cache can be audited with scan_cache_dir, L680, which reports per-repo and per-revision disk usage. Between them, hf_raise_for_status, L826 turns HTTP errors into typed, actionable exceptions — the difference between a cryptic 412 and a message that tells you a revision does not exist.

Inference and the Wider Ecosystem

HfFileSystem, L370 is the module power users grow to love: it implements the fsspec abstract filesystem over Hub URLs, so libraries that accept “any fsspec path” accept hf://datasets/... for free. Its file classes stream over the same HTTP layer, and metadata_load, L515-style helpers in repocard.py round out the story with typed access to README front-matter — RepoCard, L37 parses and writes the YAML metadata that makes model cards machine-readable.

For running models rather than fetching them, InferenceClient, L124 fronts Hugging Face’s Inference Providers with methods like chat_completion, L531 and text_to_image; infrastructure-level deployments have their own client in _inference_endpoints.py. And if your library wants to piggyback on all of this, PyTorchModelHubMixin, L692 gives any nn.Module save_pretrained/from_pretrained semantics for free — that is the exact hook transformers and friends build on.

Honest Limits

A tour should also say what the code does not do:

  • It is a client, not an engine. huggingface_hub moves files and calls remote APIs; it never runs a model locally. Downloads land on disk; executing them is the job of libraries like transformers.
  • Inference needs a server somewhere. InferenceClient talks to hosted Inference Providers or your own endpoint — there is no local execution mode hiding in the client.
  • Some features need extras. The README notes the package stays minimal by default; for example the MCP module requires pip install "huggingface_hub[mcp]". Xet upload also activates based on what the Hub reports per file — it is negotiated, not unconditional.
  • The cache layout is symlink-based. Snapshot files link back into blobs, which is efficient and deduplicated, but means tools that do not follow links (or filesystems with link restrictions) need the local_dir mode instead.
  • Line numbers drift. Everything here is pinned to main as of 2026-10-30; the codebase moves fast — bucket storage, jobs, and sandbox modules are recent arrivals — so re-grep before citing exact lines.

If you want to keep pulling on this thread, the natural companions are the tokenizer implementation in tokenizers, the safetensors weight format in safetensors, and the dataset loading machinery in datasets — together they complete the picture of what actually happens between pip install and a tensor on your GPU.
entry.summary: A line-anchored tour through huggingface_hub's source: downloads, commit operations, cache layout, auth, and inference, each traced to real code.

entry.title: MLflow Source Tour: From Fluent API to Backend Stores and the Model Registry

link.title: MLflow Source Tour: From Fluent API to Backend Stores and the Model Registry

entry.content:
MLflow describes itself on its README as “The Open Source AI Engineering Platform for Agents, LLMs & Models,” and the claim is not marketing fluff: the project reports over 60 million monthly downloads, and the repository is one of the largest Python codebases in the ML tooling ecosystem. Most developers meet MLflow through three lines of code — start_run, log_param, log_metric — and never think about what happens after the function returns. That gap between the friendly API and the machinery underneath is exactly what this source tour covers. We cloned the mlflow/mlflow repository at master, read the tracking, storage, and model-packaging layers, and mapped the real call routes into two architecture diagrams that link every node to the actual source file on GitHub.

The interesting engineering story here is the layering. MLflow exposes a thin fluent module (mlflow/tracking/fluent.py) that keeps global state for your script, a full client class (MlflowClient) for programmatic use, an internal service client that owns the backend abstraction, and then two completely different storage backends — a plain filesystem store and a SQLAlchemy-backed database store — behind a tiny URI dispatch function. On top of all of that sit “flavors” like mlflow.sklearn and the generic pyfunc loader, plus a model registry with its own storage layer. Because every layer is a separate file with a clear seam, reading the source is genuinely pleasant, and the same seams are where you would intervene if you wanted to add a custom backend or a new flavor.

The diagram below is the 10,000-foot view: your script and the CLI on the left, the service and REST server in the middle, the stores and entities at the bottom right, and the model packaging path on the right edge. Each node is clickable and opens the exact file in the GitHub repository at the master branch, so you can treat this page as a navigable index into the codebase rather than a static picture.

MLflow overview — the fluent facade, the client layer, the store dispatch, both backend stores, the registry, and the model packaging path. Every node links to its source file at master.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Fluent facade. set_experiment, L144 and start_run, L449 in mlflow/tracking/fluent.py are what you call in a script; start_run returns an ActiveRun that doubles as a context manager, with end_run, L718 and active_run, L771 managing the global current-run pointer.
  • Full client. MlflowClient, L245 in mlflow/tracking/client.py exposes the same operations without global state — for example create_run, L603, which the docstring explicitly contrasts with start_run: it creates the object but does not touch the “active run” used by log_param.
  • Service layer. TrackingServiceClient, L83 is the internal workhorse, with create_run, L159, log_metric, L335, and log_batch, L507 delegating to whichever store was resolved.
  • URI dispatch. set_tracking_uri, L69 records where data should go, and _get_store, L265 in the same file resolves that URI through a registry of schemes to a concrete store instance.
  • File backend. FileStore, L221 in mlflow/store/tracking/file_store.py is the zero-setup default: runs, params, metrics, and artifacts live as YAML and text files under a directory like ./mlruns.
  • Database backend. SqlAlchemyStore, L370 backs sqlite, postgres, and mysql URIs with implementations like create_run, L1080, log_metric, L1391, and log_batch, L2428.
  • Server and CLI. The mlflow server command is defined at server, L554 and boots the REST handlers built by _run_server, L450; the README’s own quickstart is simply uvx mlflow server plus mlflow.set_tracking_uri("http://localhost:5000").
  • Model packaging. Model, L402 is the MLmodel metadata object (serialized by save, L776), and flavors like mlflow.sklearn.log_model, L394 build on it.

From Install to Your First Model

Everything in this section is straight from the README’s three-step quickstart and the fluent module itself. Install first:

pip install mlflow

Start the server exactly as the README suggests (uvx mlflow server is the zero-install variant; with pip you can run mlflow server from the same command class):

mlflow server

Then point your script at it and turn on autologging — the README example uses mlflow.openai.autolog(), and equivalent autolog functions exist for other frameworks. If you prefer the explicit, framework-neutral form, the fluent API is three calls:

import mlflow

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("http://localhost:5000")
mlflow.set_experiment("first-steps")

with mlflow.start_run(run_name="hello-mlflow") as run:
    mlflow.log_param("learning_rate", 0.01)
    mlflow.log_metric("accuracy", 0.93, step=1)

print(run.info.run_id)

What happens under the hood when that with block exits? start_run resolves an experiment, asks the client for a run, and stores the resulting ActiveRun as the global current run. log_param and log_metric look up that active run and route through MlflowClient into the service client. When the context manager exits, end_run calls set_terminated (L788), which stamps the run’s end time and status. If you skipped the server entirely and never called set_tracking_uri, the URI resolver falls back to the local FileStore — the README promises “no complex setup,” and the code honors that by making the filesystem backend the default.

Packaging a trained model is the second half of the story. Calling mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, "model") inside a run does three things: it constructs a Model object holding the flavor, signature, and the run ID that produced it (see self.run_id at L428); it writes the estimator plus an MLmodel descriptor as artifacts via fluent.log_artifact, L1637; and if you passed registered_model_name, it asks the registry to pin that artifact as a new version. Loading it back is symmetric: mlflow.pyfunc.load_model, L1081 reads the MLmodel file, picks the right loader, and hands you a callable, while mlflow.sklearn.load_model, L741 delegates to pyfunc and restores the original estimator object.

Inside the Client Layer

The split between fluent.py and client.py is deliberate and worth copying in your own designs. The fluent module owns conversation state — which experiment is active, which run is current — while MlflowClient is stateless from the caller’s perspective. Both funnel into TrackingServiceClient, but they reach it differently: the fluent module lazily constructs its client on first use (the import of MlflowClient sits at L104 of fluent.py), while MlflowClient creates its service client in the constructor. The batch entry point MlflowClient.log_batch, L2733 is what autologgers call: metrics, params, and tags go up in one request instead of dozens.

The URI dispatch in utils.py is the seam that makes all backends interchangeable. set_tracking_uri stores the string; _get_store consults a TrackingStoreRegistry (defined around L236) that maps URI schemes to factory functions — empty and file: schemes go to FileStore, database schemes go to SqlAlchemyStore, and additional schemes are registered for REST, Databricks, and Unity Catalog endpoints. Registering a new backend is a one-line registry call, which is why the ecosystem has been able to add remote backends without touching the fluent layer at all.

Backend Stores: Two Implementations, One Contract

Both stores extend the same abstract contract, and the entities they exchange are plain Python dataclasses in mlflow/entities: Run, L14, RunInfo, L34, Metric, L12, and Param, L9. SqlAlchemyStore.create_run inserts a row and stamps the RunInfo status fields; log_metric (L1391) upserts into a metric history keyed by run, key, step, and timestamp so that series grow append-only; log_batch wraps metrics, params, and tags in a single managed session. Internal helpers like _get_run, L1127 enforce run existence and active-state checks before writes.

FileStore is the honest-to-goodness reference implementation: the same operations produce the same entity objects, but they materialize as a directory tree of YAML files. That is what makes mlruns/ folders so easy to inspect by hand — there is no magic, just the contract expressed as text. The cost is concurrency: the file backend is single-writer by nature, which is precisely why the server path routes everything through the database store once you graduate from a laptop.

Models, Flavors, and the Registry

The detail diagram zooms into the packaging path. A flavor is just a module that knows how to serialize one framework’s objects and register a matching loader; mlflow/sklearn/__init__.py shows the pattern end to end with log_model at L394 and load_model at L741. The base class for custom Python inference code is PythonModel, L264 in mlflow/pyfunc/model.py, paired with a PythonModelContext, L405 that hands your code the artifacts directory at load time. Because every flavor is also loadable through the generic pyfunc loader, a model written once can be served by anything that understands MLmodel — including the server routes built in mlflow/server/__init__.py.

The registry has its own storage module under mlflow/store/model_registry/, with create_registered_model, L380 and create_model_version, L982 in the SQLAlchemy implementation. A model version is essentially a pointer: it records the name, the version number, and the run_id it came from, so lineage from experiment to promotable artifact is a database join, not a convention. For teams that only need experiment tracking, the registry stays dormant; for teams promoting models across environments, it is the piece that turns “the artifact in run abc123” into “champion@v7.”

Honest Limits

A few things we deliberately did not claim. First, we did not benchmark anything: the 60-million-downloads figure is quoted from the README, and no performance numbers in this post come from our own measurements. Second, MLflow is far bigger than what fits in two diagrams — the tree lists tracing, evaluation, prompt management, an AI gateway, and deployment tooling alongside tracking, and we only toured the tracking-plus-models core that most source readers start with. Third, the backend landscape extends beyond the two stores we mapped: the dispatch registry also wires REST, Databricks, and Unity Catalog stores, which we mention but did not walk through. Fourth, MLflow Projects (mlflow.projects.run at L209) can reproduce an entire script from a MLproject file, and we link it for completeness without exploring its execution machinery. Finally, tags like mlflow.runName (defined, L11) are the glue between UI and API, but the UI’s own frontend lives outside the Python package we checked out.

If you are evaluating this stack against alternatives, it helps to read sibling tours: our Langfuse source tour covers LLM-native observability and tracing, TorchServe and TensorFlow Serving cover the serving half of the story that MLflow leaves to integrations, and Streamlit is the quickest way to build a review UI on top of logged runs. Between those and this tour you will have covered the full “train, track, package, serve” arc.
